Don’t miss Carty-Williams in conversation about the singular pressures of 30-something womanhood and why she just couldn’t quit the character that launched her writing career. Chaired by Sarah Gwonyoma.

events.title: Music and Making with Wild Wings of Hope
events.blurb: Did you know there’s a bird called a swift which travels all the way from Edinburgh to Africa every year? Amazing, right? Join Wild Wings of Hope for a delightful drop in session packed with stories, papercrafts, and drumming inspired by those brilliant wee birds. With Scottish artist Ed Harrison and Ghanaian storyteller and musician Chief Gift Amu.

events.title: The Front List: Charlie Mackesy
events.blurb: Charlie Mackesy’s bestselling illustrated book The Boy, the Mole, the Fox, and the Horse (and its Academy Award-winning BBC animation) gifted readers a timely reminder of the beauty, hope, and comfort which can be found in the world around us – and, most of all, within one another. Charlie joins us to celebrate his newest book Always Remember: The Boy, the Mole, the Fox, the Horse and the Storm, about this very special group of friends. This event, with live drawing and a discussion on where the characters are now, is for everyone. Chaired by Cathy MacDonald.

events.title: Have Lunch with Jess Elliott Dennison
events.blurb: Crispy fennel and lemon bhajis. Courgette and ricotta lasagne. Jess Elliott Dennison is at the peak of her creative powers in Vegetable Recipes, and today she brings her knack for Earth-grown deliciousness to the very place her ideas begin. Join Elliott Dennison in her Studio as she shares the endless possibilities of simple, seasonal cooking, all while creating you an utterly sumptuous lunch. Ticket includes: a welcome drink, a generous multi-course lunch, and paired wine on the table.

events.title: In a Monster Pickle with Rong Rong
events.blurb: Twiggy the Log Monster’s planning a sleepover - and you’re invited! It’s the funnest party ever, so get set for heaps of hilarious hijinks with Rong Rong’s Jolly Monster Town: The Party Pickle. Hear all about Ralph the Pufferfish Monster and Uno the Cyclops Cat, then get crafty (and a bit dafty) with Rong Rong as you dream up a friendly monster together. An event that’s big on creative play. Be there or be square!

events.title: Music and Making with Wild Wings of Hope
events.blurb: Did you know there’s a bird called a swift which travels all the way from Edinburgh to Africa every year? Amazing, right? Join Wild Wings of Hope for a delightful drop in session packed with stories, papercrafts, and drumming inspired by those brilliant wee birds. With Scottish artist Ed Harrison and Ghanaian storyteller and musician Chief Gift Amu.

events.title: Howard Cunnell & Blake Morrison: A Life Observed
events.blurb: Blake Morrison and Howard Cunnell are masters of the everyday, balancing honesty and care in equal measure. Morrison’s On Memoir: An A-Z of Life Writing offers delightful musings on the art of narrative non-fiction, while his poetry collection Afterburn illuminates the small intimacies that bind us to others. Cunnell’s Sun Country, meanwhile, is a luminous memoir journeying from sorrow to acceptance. They join us to discuss these tender books about stories, memory, and family histories. Chaired by Di Speirs.

events.title: Who Am I? with Jacqueline Wilson
events.blurb: The creator of Tracy Beaker hardly needs any introduction – Jacqueline Wilson is literally a legend. Back at the Festival after a sold out show last year, she brings us her latest book, Esme Pepper – if Tracy was loudly ‘this is my life!’, Esme is more ‘Who am I, and where do I fit?’ The Jacqueline Wilson story stardust is as sparkly as ever, and today she’ll take us into the heart of how she weaves her unique magic. Jacqueline megafans assemble!

events.title: Richard Collett & Andrew Hussey: Talking to Strangers
events.blurb: Do we have more in common than that which divides us? In their latest works, Andrew Hussey (Fractured France: Journey Through a Divided Nation) and Richard Collett (Along the Borders: In Search of What Divides and Unites the British Isles) travelled through France and Britain, talking to strangers to find the heart of each nation. Today, they share stories of their conversations – from the profound to the ridiculous – reflecting on what brings us all together. Chaired by Jemma Neville.

events.title: Deep Listening: A Workshop with Emily Kasriel
events.blurb: In a society where empathetic dialogue feels increasingly rare, BBC journalist, executive coach, and mediator Emily Kasriel has developed Deep Listening: a transformative practice that moves beyond surface-level conversation to create genuine connection, foster authentic expression, and open pathways to understanding – even when we profoundly disagree. In this interactive workshop, Kasriel will demonstrate this innovative approach and give participants a chance to put it into practice and consider its potential in their own lives.

events.title: Poorna Bell: She Wanted More
events.blurb: She Wanted More is Poorna Bell’s urgent and wise exploration of women who have shunned society’s ‘rules’ to forge their own paths, no longer settling for what others expect across careers, romance, motherhood, and more. Join Bell today, alongside podcaster Sam Baker and poet Hollie McNish, as they lead an expectation-busting rallying cry to reimagine our own roadmaps and to know that, at any age, we can reshape our futures. Chaired by Anahit Behrooz.

events.title: Music and Making with Wild Wings of Hope
events.blurb: Did you know there’s a bird called a swift which travels all the way from Edinburgh to Africa every year? Amazing, right? Join Wild Wings of Hope for a delightful drop in session packed with stories, papercrafts, and drumming inspired by those brilliant wee birds. With Scottish artist Ed Harrison and Ghanaian storyteller and musician Chief Gift Amu.

events.title: Know Your Gnomes with Loes Riphagen
events.blurb: Want to know what gnomes eat, what pets they keep, what disguises they wear? You’re about to become an expert! Delve deep into the weird and wonderful world of gnomes, as author-illustrator Loes Riphagen shares her fabulously fact-packed masterpiece: The Gnome Book. Hear gnome-tastic stories, take part in gnome-ific craft activities, and even receive a Little Gnome Diploma at the end. For miniature-size magic, it’s a must!

events.title: Ione Gamble & Philippa Snow: Icons Only
events.blurb: In It's Terrible the Things I Have to Do to Be Me, Philippa Snow gives us a radical study of female icons through pairs of famous women. It’s full of the glamour and debauchery of Hollywood, just like Ione Gamble’s The Polyester Book of (Bad) Taste: a deep dive into the joy and power of personal pleasures, quirks, obsessions, and bad taste. Join the duo’s discussion on pop culture, exposure, punishment, and the gruelling demands of femininity and fame. Chaired by Tomiwa Folorunso.

events.title: Music and Making with Wild Wings of Hope
events.blurb: Did you know there’s a bird called a swift which travels all the way from Edinburgh to Africa every year? Amazing, right? Join Wild Wings of Hope for a delightful drop in session packed with stories, papercrafts, and drumming inspired by those brilliant wee birds. With Scottish artist Ed Harrison and Ghanaian storyteller and musician Chief Gift Amu.

events.title: Animal Magic with Hannah Gold
events.blurb: Hannah Gold’s adventure stories, including her latest The Lone Husky, have one thing in common – the call of the Arctic wild. April Wood made friends with a polar bear in The Last Bear; this time, it’s a husky with a troubled past. This event’s for anyone who’s felt a connection with animals and knows how important they are. With their habitats in danger all over the world, imagine – like April – if every person did just one thing…

events.title: Fergus McIntosh: The Matter of Facts
events.blurb: In an era of post-truth, deepfakes, AI misinformation, and underfunded newsrooms, guardians of truth are more important than ever. The New Yorker’s Head Research Editor Fergus McIntosh leads an exacting, AI-free operation, which doesn’t just check every article, story, poem, cartoon, and piece of cover art for essential truth, but also has to adjudicate every day on what exactly constitutes ‘fact’ in the first place. He joins us with compelling tales from the frontline of preserving objective reality. Chaired by Lucia Osborne-Crowley.

events.title: Stephen Grosz: Love’s Labour
events.blurb: If Stephen Grosz’s bestseller The Examined Life was a guidebook for living well, Love’s Labour is a roadmap for how to love better: our friends, our families, our partners, and ourselves. Perfectly dubbed ‘the poet laureate of human emotion’ by Elizabeth Day, today the psychoanalyst shares his gift of pinpointing what ails the heartsick. Expect candid tales from the consulting room, some tricky home truths, and a whole lot of love. Chaired by Chitra Ramaswamy.

events.title: Phoenix Draw-Off: Penguins vs Donuts!
events.blurb: The Phoenix fans unite! It’s the ultimate daredevil draw-off… the epic Evil Emperor Penguin vs the dynamic Donut Squad. Who will win? Only you can decide! Join us for a Very Important and Not at All Silly competition between comic heroes Laura Ellen Anderson and Neill Cameron. Pens at the ready…!

events.title: A Mad Chatter Tea Party with Anna James
events.blurb: Ever wonder what happened when Alice emerged from the rabbit hole, grew up, and had a family of her own? Anna James’ beautiful sort-of sequel, Alice with a Why, imagines a return to Wonderland as Alice’s granddaughter finds herself among the whimsy and weirdness of her childhood stories. Hear all about it in this whimsical tea party themed event – don’t be late, don’t be late, it’s a very important date.

events.title: Schemes, Screams, and Secrets with Holly Bourne
events.blurb: If all the girls around you started screaming, would you laugh? Or would you run? From the searingly honest mind behind the Spinster Club series, YA author Holly Bourne chats today about her thrilling new novel, And Then We Screamed. Set amongst the strange goings-on in the seemingly perfect town of Maple Lakes, wannabe investigative journalist Clover (and her crush Brody) are determined to discover why their town is suddenly under an ear-splitting spell.

events.title: Close Read: The Waves by Virginia Woolf
events.blurb: In our Close Read series, a brilliant author guides you through a deep-diving discussion of a classic text or genre that’s inspired them. Think of it as an event blending friendly book club vibes with insightful study notes. Today, Brian Dillon (author of Ambivalence) unpacks Virginia Woolf’s stylistic masterpiece, The Waves – an exploration of individuality, self, and community that is regarded by many as her greatest work. Join us to discover Woolf like never before.

events.title: Julie Farrell, Fergus Murray & Lucy Rose: Someone Like Me
events.blurb: Society often puts us into boxes, watering down a diversity of experiences into one singular story. Someone Like Me says: no more. This non-fiction anthology, edited by Clem Bastow and Jo Case, offers an eclectic mix of stories from Autistic writers to expand our understanding of the Autistic experience. Join contributors Fergus Murray, Julie Farrell, and Lucy Rose as they explode stereotypes and discuss everything from intrusive thoughts and Autistic affirmation in families to stargazing and mermaids. Chaired by Lynsey Rogers.

events.title: Jacqueline Wilson: Picture Imperfect
events.blurb: For millennials everywhere, Jacqueline Wilson is cherished for creating some of our favourite childhood characters, from Tracy Beaker to Vicky Angel. Today, the icon of children’s literature introduces her latest novel for adults, Picture Imperfect – a sequel to 1999’s beloved The Illustrated Mum. In this wonderfully nostalgic, moving event, we catch up with Wilson and hear about a grown-up Dolphin Westward, torn between two possible futures, and the continued chaos of her mother Marigold. Chaired by Anahit Behrooz.

events.title: Chris Kraus: The Four Spent the Day Together
events.blurb: Against an increasingly polarised backdrop of Trumpian, right-wing politics, how can we begin to understand the America of today? With her urgent new novel, The Four Spent the Day Together, Chris Kraus offers her unflinchingly honest attempt via the histories of three generations of American lives. Join the author of modern classic I Love Dick for a conversation about repeated patterns, fresh starts, and making sense of chaos. Chaired by Harry Josephine Giles.

events.title: Lauren Elkin & Astrid Jorgensen: Raise Your Voice
events.blurb: Pitchy or pitch-perfect, our voices hold power. In Average at Best, Astrid Jorgensen details her journey from introvert to stage star, converting strangers into united musical forces at her phenomenal Pub Choir events. She joins Lauren Elkin, author of Scaffolding, Art Monsters, and Vocal Break: a fist-pumping history of how female singing voices intersect with activism. Hear Sinéad Gleeson lead a full-throated conversation, then unleash your own vocal cords under the tutelage of Jorgensen herself.

events.title: Laura Jones-Rivera & Heather McDaid: Publisher Not Found
events.blurb: They’ve published New York Times bestsellers, international stars, and countless debut authors. But after a decade of running the award-winning 404 Ink, Laura Jones-Rivera and Heather McDaid are winding down on their own terms. Publisher Not Found, part of their innovative Inklings series, is an honest, enlightening, behind-the-scenes look at what it takes to run a small press. In this celebratory conversation, the trailblazing pair discuss disruption, transparency, meaningful support, and what’s next. Chaired by Claire Sawers.

events.title: Niamh Hargan & Kiran Millwood Hargrave: Soulmates and Sliding Doors
events.blurb: A match made in heaven, Nyla Ahmad meets two contemporary writers to debate the role of fate in finding 'The One'. Niamh Hargan’s Nothing Good Happens After 2am follows rival bartenders on East London’s cocktail scene while Kiran Millwood Hargrave’s Almost Life is a tender tale of two women who meet on the steps of the Sacré-Cœur in Paris and keep meeting, again and again. If you’ve read One Day five times over, this conversation’s for you.

events.title: Harriet Tyce: Witch Trial
events.blurb: Crime writers don’t often find themselves caught in a web of deceit and treachery – but that’s exactly where author and contestant Harriet Tyce was during series four of The Traitors. A former barrister (and forever Faithful), Tyce’s gripping new title, Witch Trial, finds an 18-year-old dead in Edinburgh’s Inverleith Park – and her best friends charged with murder. Join Tyce to discuss modern day witch-hunts and obsessions, and whether she’s been inspired by her duplicitous co-stars. Chaired by Bryan Burnett.

events.title: Michael Pollan & Daniel Yon: Considering Consciousness [ANIL SETH has cancelled]
events.blurb: In A World Appears and Being You, Michael Pollan and Anil Seth ask one of the biggest questions there is: how does consciousness happen? From brain labs to Buddhist caves, controlled hallucinations to psychedelic revelation, Pollan - the endlessly inquisitive author of How to Change Your Mind - joins leading neuroscientist Seth to discuss Seth’s groundbreaking theory of consciousness, alongside perception, reality, selfhood, and the limits of objective neuroscience in explaining who we are. Please note: Michael Pollan will join remotely. Chaired by Ben Alderson-Day.

events.title: Evelyn Clarke: The Ending Writes Itself
events.blurb: Beginnings are tough, but endings can be murderous – just ask V E Schwab (internationally bestselling author) and Cat Clarke (acclaimed YA author and screenwriter). Joining forces as Evelyn Clarke, the longtime pals-turned-literary-double-act share The Ending Writes Itself: their fiendishly clever joint-debut featuring six writers, a private island, and a life-changing publishing opportunity that might turn deadly. Today, the pair get into the nitty gritty of mystery, satirising their own industry, and the fun of co-writing 2026’s most hotly anticipated thriller. Chaired by Cailean Steed.

events.title: 10 Years After David Bowie: Sound & Visions
events.blurb: Ten years since we lost David Bowie, journalist and broadcaster Nicola Meighan hosts an exuberant evening celebrating the music, writing, iconography, theatrical worlds, and cinematic wonder of the Thin White Duke. Expect Bowie covers from brilliant artists such as Lung Leg, and some very special guests reflecting on the impact of Ziggy Stardust, Aladdin Sane, and the wild and trailblazing work of the man who fell to earth, then fired it up.

events.title: Are You Sitting Comfortably?
events.blurb: Join us for a relaxed morning story especially for your littlest readers with Anne Brusatte.

events.title: Emily Kasriel & Gabrielle Rifkind: Radical Listening and Managing Radical Disagreements
events.blurb: How do we connect and really hear each other amid the cacophony of our world? Former BBC journalist, mediator, and executive coach Emily Kasriel and world-leading conflict mediator and psychologist Gabrielle Rifkind have some ideas. They join us to discuss Deep Listening and How to Agree to Disagree, both expert guides for tackling conflict in the modern day, exploring how to empower yourself (even when in fierce disagreement), increase empathy, and foster understanding across divides. Chaired by Alisha Fernandez Miranda.

events.title: First Edition
events.blurb: Start your day with the facts. High quality, thorough, trustworthy journalism has never been more important in helping us understand the world as it really is – but we know how hard it can be to keep up. That’s what our First Edition events are for: offering you the chance to join leading journalists from across the media (and the world) as they discuss the day’s breaking news over a cup of coffee. The line-up includes Michael MacLeod (The Minute), Phyllis Stephen (founder of Edinburgh Reporter, owner of Deadline News) & Jane Bradley (Arts Correspondent at The Scotsman).

events.title: Pop in and Play
events.blurb: Come and play with us! Everyone is welcome for our 30-minute guided sessions of fun and games, ideal to keep your wee ones busy. We know that great stories can come from great playtimes (no matter your age) so on your marks… get set… imagine!

events.title: Shared Reading with Open Book
events.blurb: Join Open Book Lead Readers for an informal and relaxed shared reading session. Each session will explore a chapter from a debut book from this year’s Festival programme. No experience necessary, all reading materials will be provided on the day.

events.title: Scots Bookbug with Scots Language Centre
events.blurb: Bring yer wee yins alang fir a Scots Bookbug wi sangs, rhymes, an stories. Abody’s welcome, whither ye’re a gallus Scots speaker or a wee feartie!

events.title: Train Tales
events.blurb: Let's take a train to Imagination Land! Join our pals from LNER for Train Tales, a chance to hop aboard for stories and brilliant activities to help little ones get ready for future journeys. There might even be a very special guest...

events.title: Stephen McGinty: One Morning in March
events.blurb: On 13 March 1996, at Dunblane Primary School, 16 pupils and one teacher were murdered, and many more injured, in the deadliest mass shooting in British history. The crime didn’t just shock the nation, it changed it – but only after an extraordinary political battle by a group of grieving parents determined that the atrocity would never be repeated. Journalist and BAFTA award-winning documentarian Stephen McGinty, author of One Morning in March, reveals the story of that devastating day, the troubling events which preceded it, and its lasting legacy. Chaired by Laura Miller.

events.title: Erica Wagner: Wash
events.blurb: Erica Wagner brings us Wash, one of the most critically acclaimed historical novels of 2026. Reimagining the life of ﻿Washington 'Augustus' Roebling, the man who oversaw the building of the iconic Brooklyn Bridge, the book is something of an ‘anti-biography’. Meet Wagner today – a literary personality of truly polymathic range – to discover how a singular but little-known life can unspool themes of growth, yearning, the price of achievement, and roads not taken. Chaired by Lee Randall.

events.title: Scots Bookbug with Scots Language Centre
events.blurb: Bring yer wee yins alang fir a Scots Bookbug wi sangs, rhymes, an stories. Abody’s welcome, whither ye’re a gallus Scots speaker or a wee feartie!

events.title: Hannah French: The Rolling Year
events.blurb: Eating with the seasons is one thing, but have you ever tuned your ear to them? Dr Hannah French did while writing The Rolling Year: Listening to the Seasons with Vivaldi. Today the BBC Radio 3 presenter and musicologist shares her fresh perspective on one of the world’s most cherished musical scores, drawing from experts in science, health, food, and more. 300 years on, what can Vivaldi still teach us about the beauty and brutality of nature? Chaired by Kate Molleson.

events.title: Pop in and Play
events.blurb: Come and play with us! Everyone is welcome for our 30-minute guided sessions of fun and games, ideal to keep your wee ones busy. We know that great stories can come from great playtimes (no matter your age) so on your marks… get set… imagine!

events.title: Oliver Bullough & Caroline Knowles: Dirty Money
events.blurb: Our cities are built and rebuilt on the billions of private investors. Funds are pumped in, shifted around, and squirrelled away – movements that have been closely scrutinised by Oliver Bullough and Caroline Knowles in their new books Everybody Loves Our Dollars and Uneasy Streets. Where Bullough discusses just how much of the world’s GDP is ‘dirty’, Knowles explores the impact on the ground, as developments are left unfinished when political tides turn and investment dries up.

events.title: The Front List: David Olusoga
events.blurb: Author, broadcaster, historian, and The Celebrity Traitors’ ultimate Faithful, David Olusoga has been pivotal in broadening the scope of British history. Through titles including Black and British: A Forgotten History, and TV series like Britain’s Forgotten Slave Owners and the beloved A House Through Time (whose latest series features a property on Edinburgh’s Calton Hill), he’s exposed racial injustice throughout history, and told a more honest, comprehensive story of our past. Today he reflects on his impressive career and what’s still to be achieved. Chaired by Amina Shah.

events.title: Marina Warner: Sanctuary
events.blurb: What is ‘sanctuary’? Is it a sacred place where travellers and refugees might find safety and solace? Or is it a homeland to be shuttered and defended against incomers from the outside world? Exploring the concept throughout history and myth in her book Sanctuary, prolific critic, cultural historian, and Booker Prize-shortlisted novelist Marina Warner joins us today to ask profound and urgent questions about the right to safety, home, freedom of movement, and peace. Chaired by Charlotte Higgins.

events.title: Close Read: In Cold Blood by Truman Capote
events.blurb: In our Close Read series, a brilliant author guides you through a deep-diving discussion of a classic text or genre that’s inspired them. Think of it as an event blending friendly book club vibes with insightful study notes. Today, Chris Kraus (author of I Love Dick and The Four Spent the Day Together) turns her critic’s gaze on In Cold Blood, Truman Capote’s true-crime trailblazer. Together, uncover the layers of Capote’s controversial, compelling non-fiction novel.

events.title: John Lanchester: Look What You Made Me Do
events.blurb: Picture settling down to watch the year’s buzziest TV show, only to realise it’s based on the toe-curling details of your own marriage. That’s the premise behind Look What You Made Me Do, John Lanchester’s darkly funny jaunt through the resentments and entitlements of the middle classes – his first novel since Booker-longlisted The Wall. Dan Richards chats to him about our public and private faces and the differences that pull taut between generations.

events.title: Peter Ross: Journeys in Ancient Britain and Ireland
events.blurb: Ancient places, structures, and monuments can be key sites of wonder and wondering, as Peter Ross finds in Upon A White Horse. Combining historical research and archaeological insights with fascinating stories, the bestselling, prize-winning author of Steeple Chasing journeys through Britain and Ireland's prehistoric sites, drawing on their influence on our art, culture, and society. Today, he discusses his travels, his findings (including a wooden goddess in Edinburgh), and the mysteries encountered along the way. Chaired by Caroline Eden.

events.title: Pop in and Play
events.blurb: Come and play with us! Everyone is welcome for our 30-minute guided sessions of fun and games, ideal to keep your wee ones busy. We know that great stories can come from great playtimes (no matter your age) so on your marks… get set… imagine!

events.title: John Curtice: Is Two-Party Politics Over?
events.blurb: Sir John Curtice, Professor of Politics at the University of Strathclyde, has become known as one of our most incisive, animated, and well-regarded political commentators on TV through his clear and knowledgeable translations of polling data. In the wake of election results across Scotland, England, and Wales – which saw distinct shifts in voting and political power – he shares his view on the status of the two party political system at Westminster, and how its demise would herald the biggest change in our electoral landscape since the 1920s.

events.title: David Turner: A History of Resistance
events.blurb: Those who write the history books shape the stories we come to know – but who gets left out? It’s something historian and professor David Turner considers in Disability: A History of Resistance. Spanning centuries of British history, Turner unearths not just historic hardships, but also untold narratives of resistance, resourcefulness, and resilience excluded from mainstream accounts. Hear Turner reflect on how understanding our nation’s past offers us the opportunity to create a truly inclusive future. Chaired by Louise Brangan.

events.title: Kathy Lette: The Sisterhood Rules
events.blurb: Veteran bon vivant Kathy Lette has a knack for bringing levity to life’s curveballs. Her new novel, The Sisterhood Rules – called ‘deliciously rude and darkly funny’ by Nicole Kidman – follows twins whose bond is shattered when one has an affair with the other's husband. Forced to co-operate when their mother goes missing, it’s a romp through the bumpy terrain of siblinghood. Lette joins Jenny Colgan for a natter about lust, loyalty, and the ties that bind us.

events.title: Brigid Collins & Christine De Luca: Such Fragile Futures
events.blurb: What does it mean to bring tender attention to our encounters with nature? Join artist Brigid Collins and poet Christine De Luca as they unfold their year-long creative collaboration in Dr Neil’s Garden beside Edinburgh’s Duddingston Loch. With readings from Such Fragile Futures: An Artist and a Poet Reflect in a Garden, and artworks so sensuous you want to reach out and touch them, discover how humans might begin healing our world. Chaired by Dr Kitty Wheater.

events.title: Benjamin Wood: Seascraper
events.blurb: A tang of sea salt in the air, and a thundering wave of acclaim – buckle up for an encounter with Benjamin Wood’s Nero Book Award-winning and Booker Prize-longlisted Seascraper, a novel that challenges the limits of literary realism. Today, hear Wood chatting with us about his haunting world, where a young, duty-bound shrimp-fisherman is offered a tantalising out. You’ll feel the razorshells crunch underfoot in this conversation that asks: Can we ever, really, break free? Chaired by Sinéad Gleeson.

events.title: Pop in and Play
events.blurb: Come and play with us! Everyone is welcome for our 30-minute guided sessions of fun and games, ideal to keep your wee ones busy. We know that great stories can come from great playtimes (no matter your age) so on your marks… get set… imagine!

events.title: Y M Abdel-Magied & Meena Kandasamy: Putting the World to Rights
events.blurb: Author, screenwriter, and award-winning social advocate Y M Abdel-Magied joins poet, activist, and novelist Meena Kandasamy for a galvanising conversation about principles and power dynamics in a divided world. In At Sea, Abdel-Magied draws on her past life as a drilling engineer to confront urgent questions about the cost of human ambition, while Kandasamy’s Fieldwork as a Sex Object follows the fuse from online incel threats to offline nationalist violence. Two clear-eyed commentators in their element. Chaired by Nicola Sturgeon.

events.title: Oliver Bullough: Everybody Loves Our Dollars
events.blurb: Following his oligarch-busting Butler to the World, Oliver Bullough returns to hang the world’s dirty money out to dry. In Everybody Loves Our Dollars, Bullough suggests there’s never been a better time to be a criminal in the UK. Moving and hiding money couldn’t be easier, and despite efforts to legislate, it’s estimated as much as 5% of world GDP is on the grubbier side. This revelatory conversation brings a murky underworld into razor-sharp focus. Chaired by Paul French.

events.title: Kapka Kassabova: Borrowed Land
events.blurb: What does it mean to truly fight for your home when faced with the forces of colonialism, industry, and depopulation? In Borrowed Land, Kapka Kassabova draws a stunning portrait of the Scottish Highlands, telling the epic and urgent stories of the last true Highlanders and their battle for preservation. Today, the award-winning writer, whose recent Balkan quartet concluded with the spellbinding Anima, delves into the extraordinary, centuries-old connections between the land, nature, and people. Chaired by Angus Peter Campbell.

events.title: Communities Cabaret: Changing Your Mind
events.blurb: We’ve challenged local writers and poets to respond to this year’s Festival theme: Changing Your Mind. Join us as we bring them together to perform their work and create a patchwork of ideas on trying new things, listening to different perspectives, and keeping a sense of wonder in our ever-changing world. You can expect a diverse, thought-provoking, and energising evening of live music, poetry, and storytelling.

events.title: Doug Johnstone: Ghost Notes
events.blurb: Ghost Notes is the latest instalment in Doug Johnstone’s addictive series following the Skelf women: three generations of funeral-directors-turned-private-investigators. This time, they’re thrown into the murky world of ‘grief tech’, a booming industry that creates digital avatars of the dead. Hear one of Scotland’s most reliably entertaining authors – now in his 20th year of publishing – reflect on his career so far and chat about writing the death industry with characteristic humour, insight, and heart. Chaired by Mary Paulson-Ellis.

events.title: Frank Dikötter: Red Dawn Over China
events.blurb: Over a century ago, the Chinese Communist Party emerged as a band of radical, Soviet Union-backed countryside insurgents. Now, it presides over one of the world’s major economic, technological, and military powers, with a population of 1.4 billion. Isabel Hilton talks to leading China historian and Samuel Johnson Prize-winner Frank Dikötter about his gripping new history, Red Dawn Over China, unpacking China’s path to Communism and how it shaped the world we know today.

events.title: Nonomiya/Song of Rona Island
events.blurb:
As part of Scotland to the World, we bring you a unique fusion of Japanese and Scottish culture. Rarely experienced outside its home country, Noh is a 600-year-old form of classical Japanese musical drama, into which the experimental Noh Reimagined theatre company is breathing new life. 


They bring us today’s two-part performance, introducing Noh Theatre in Part One with a piece based on the oldest novel of all time, followed by a new and contemporary collaboration blending Scottish and Japanese folklore, myth and music in Part Two. 

This performance is repeated on Tue 25 Aug at 19:00

Part One: Nonomiya (Wildwood Shrine) (15th century) 
Nonomiya is a masterwork of Noh theatre, written by Konparu Zenchiku in the 15th century, based on the 11th century classic, The Tale of Genji by Murasaki Shikibu. This performance presents the famous second act, in which the spirit of Lady Rokujō reveals her lingering passion and sorrow. 


Part Two: Song of Rona Island (2025) 
A once-in-a-lifetime chance to experience the groundbreaking union of Scottish culture and the 600-year-old art of Japanese Noh theatre, inspired by former Makar Kathleen Jamie’s essay ‘On Rona’ from her collection, Sightlines. Through dialogue, chant, dance, and music, five Noh performers and Scots musicians Aidan O’Rourke and Brìghde Chaimbeul take us on an ecological journey to an abandoned Hebridean island to discover its haunting past.
Line-up includes Kanji Shimizu, Takao Nishimura, Kyosuke Tanabe, Satoshi Tsukitaku, Keinosuke Okura, Aidan O’Rourke & Brighde Chaimbeul.
Part of Scotland to the World. Supported by Sir Ewan and Lady Brown, The British Council, The Great Britain Sasakawa Foundation, and TESSENKAI

events.title: Brian Dillon: Ambivalence
events.blurb: For many of us, reading is more than a syllabus – it is sustenance. In Ambivalence, boundary-breaking essayist Brian Dillon looks back on his formative years in Dublin, tracing an education shaped less by classrooms than by books, grief, and radical ideas. The acclaimed author of Essayism discusses the seductions of ambiguity and how reading freethinking writers like Woolf, Beckett, Benjamin, and Barthes gave form to a mind devoted to the process of becoming. Chaired by Charlotte Higgins.

events.title: Jason Burke: The Revolutionists
events.blurb: In the 1970s a new breed of charismatic and violent extremists publicised their causes before a global audience through hijackings, hostage-taking, and terrorist bombing campaigns – the attention tactics they employed have never gone away. Today the Guardian’s international security correspondent Jason Burke discusses The Revolutionists, his thrilling, unsettling secret history of the decade through profiles of unpredictable anti-West characters including Leila Khaled, Carlos the Jackal, and the Baader-Meinhof gang. Chaired by Allan Little.

events.title: Åsne Seierstad: Russian Lives at War
events.blurb: In an at-war nation which has shut down dissent and reportage, how can we glimpse behind the curtain? Discussing Unpeace: Russian Lives at War, Åsne Seierstad (author of The Bookseller of Kabul and called ‘the supreme non-fiction writer of her generation’) draws upon the testimony of Wagner Group defector Andrey Medvedev and her own time living in Russia to craft an intimate yet far-reaching, unflinching portrait of Russian life in the Putin age. Chaired by Peter Godwin.

events.title: Immortalising Sisterhood: The Salon (Natasha Cottriall has cancelled).
events.blurb:
Please also see updated copy: 
Connection lies at the heart of sisterhood and tonight, Gemma Cairney takes over the Speigeltent for a cabaret-style evening of music, conversation and good vibes. Come and enjoy a drink, take a seat at the table and engage in the magic of Cairney and her guests Candice Carty-Williams, Lake Montgomery, Camara Lundestad, and Naomi Shimada as they explore themes of the radical, art lovin' and everything in-between. Get your flowers and make a crown, and feel free to wear your celebratory glad-rags!

events.title: Are You Sitting Comfortably?
events.blurb: Join us for a relaxed morning story especially for your littlest readers. Appearing today: Naomi Tipping.

events.title: First Edition: PEN International
events.blurb: Start your day with the facts. In 2025, the 91st PEN International Congress in Kraków passed a resolution on the role of writers during a breakdown of peace and international order, and the urgent need for an active opposition. Today, Viv Groskop (PEN International Writers Circle) speaks to writers and journalists – including Sabrin Hasbun, and Tahmima Anam  – about the vital role of writers to defend facts, propel empathy, and hold governments accountable in a time of authoritarianism, disinformation, and inequality.

events.title: Pop in and Play with Edinburgh for Under Fives
events.blurb: The team from Edinburgh for Under Fives are back to entertain little ones with a story and art activity to take home. Come along to the tent for 30 minutes of guided fun!

events.title: How to Talk Across Divides: A Workshop with Sarah Stein Lubrano
events.blurb: Researcher and author of Don't Talk About Politics: How to Change 21st-Century Minds, Sarah Stein Lubrano knows why most conversations achieve nothing, as well as why a few have changed the world. In today’s workshop, Stein Lubrano will guide participants of diverse viewpoints and opinions through how to approach conversations with openness, curiosity, and strategy, using learnings from ancient philosophy to modern neuroscience to help us move beyond endless circular arguments and raised voices to considerate, constructive discussions – and hopefully positive collaboration. Democracy depends on it.

events.title: Snuggle in with Naomi Tipping
events.blurb: Cosy in for a playful making session with Naomi Tipping, whose hand-painted board books were part of the inspiration for the Little Simon installation. Dogs Get Dressed is the perfect way to start the day, while Night, Night Cats gets little ones ready for bed in the company of some very cute kittens. In this session you’ll illustrate your very own character and a little bed to tuck it into.

events.title: Fresh Words: Roundhouse Collective
events.blurb: It’s lunchtime, but there’s no need to doomscroll over your meal deal. Be the first to discover the literary stars of the future, instead. In partnership with Scottish Book Trust and other leading UK talent spotters, this lively event showcases electrifying new voices, so grab your seat before everyone else does. Today, we partner with London's Roundhouse Poetry Collective, hearing readings from an amazing line-up of poets – check back soon for the full line-up. SBT Writers: Liam Crouse, Eloise Birtwhistle. Roundhouse writers: Anna Robinson, Shermya Modupe, Ellen Waters.

events.title: Pop in and Play with Edinburgh for Under Fives
events.blurb: The team from Edinburgh for Under Fives are back to entertain little ones with a story and art activity to take home. Come along to the tent for 30 minutes of guided fun!

events.title: Kirsty Gunn, Alan Riach, and James Robertson: Scotland 1926
events.blurb: 100 years ago, Scottish literature was crackling with new energy. In this lively panel chat, Kirsty Gunn, Alan Riach, and James Robertson revisit the Scottish Renaissance through landmark works including Hugh MacDiarmid’s A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle, the early work of Neil M Gunn (newly reissued this year), and other under-sung voices including Willa Muir and Helen Cruickshank. Deep dive into a remarkable literary moment and the writers who helped reshape Scotland’s imaginative life. Chaired by Linden Bicket.

events.title: James Crawford: The Vanishing Earth
events.blurb: In our insatiable pursuit of economic growth, modern civilisation has upended the planet; our relentless extraction of resources has created environmental and social carnage. Yet, within the same landscapes experiencing the ruins of extraction, radical alternatives are emerging. Discussing his incisive new book, The Vanishing Earth, acclaimed historian, writer, and BBC Radio 4’s Take Four Books presenter James Crawford exposes the cost of endless growth on our planet and the essential actions that could save it. Chaired by Cal Flyn.

events.title: The Front List: Kiran Desai
events.blurb: After a 20-year wait, Kiran Desai returns with another spellbinding epic. Following two young lovers across continents, The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny is a sweeping love story and a dazzling meditation on class, race, migration, and the many forms of modern loneliness. This is a rare opportunity to hear the Booker-winning author of The Inheritance of Loss reflect on solitude in all its forms, and why only novels can truly get at the raw truth of human experience.

events.title: Susie Boyt: Loved and Missed
events.blurb: Published to critical acclaim in the summer of 2021, Susie Boyt’s Loved and Missed became a hand-sell favourite of booksellers, passionately recommended through a network of book-lovers and book-clubbers the whole world over. A ‘quietly heroic’ novel that explores the limits, disappointments, and excesses of love in all its forms – we’re thrilled to finally welcome Boyt to Edinburgh to discuss this gorgeous slow-burn of a book with Lisa Owens.

events.title: Angus Peter Campbell: Donald and His Seven Cows
events.blurb: Whether in English or in Gaelic, land and memory sit at the heart of Angus Peter Campbell’s absorbing, melodic writing. In Donald and His Seven Cows, Campbell explores the changes facing island life through the rituals and daily routines of Donald and his small herd, set against the vividly rendered backdrop of his native South Uist. Hear Campbell discuss the connections between land, history, folklore, and cultural memory. Chaired by Joyce McMillan.

events.title: John Lanchester & Alexander Starritt: Work/Life Balance
events.blurb: Two masters of observational fiction come together to explore why our feelings around work and money can reveal the deepest truths. Alexander Starritt’s Drayton and Mackenzie, a friendship epic about two entrepreneurs, was the first novel in 15 years to grace the Financial Times’s Business Book of the Year longlist, while John Lanchester’s black comedy, Look What You Made Me Do, poses the question: is it ever ethical to profit from another person’s pain? Chaired by Zoe Venditozzi.

events.title: Pop in and Play with Edinburgh for Under Fives
events.blurb: The team from Edinburgh for Under Fives are back to entertain little ones with a story and art activity to take home. Come along to the tent for 30 minutes of guided fun!

events.title: A C Grayling: For the People
events.blurb: The great British philosopher and academic A C Grayling’s appearances are always an intellectual highlight of the Book Festival, as he turns his forensic, yet empathetic, gaze upon defining issues of our time. This year, Grayling addresses the urgent theme of his new book, For the People, exploring how the forces of authoritarianism, election interference, and loss of faith in our institutions threaten the collapse of democracy, while offering bold suggestions for its survival.

events.title: Paul French: The Last Emperor of China
events.blurb: The road to modern China began with the 1912 abdication of the final emperor Puyi and the establishment of the People’s Republic, ending half a millennium of imperial rule from the mysterious Forbidden City. Award-winning historian of modern China, Paul French, brings all his expertise to bear in the meticulously-researched The Last Emperor of China, and today reveals the hidden story of the last days of empire and how they influenced all that followed. Chaired by James Brodie.

events.title: Lani Watson: Why Ask Questions?
events.blurb: Every once in a while, a book changes how you move through life. Q: The Hidden Power of Questions in a World that Wants Answers is one of those books: a revelatory examination, by philosopher Lani Watson, of the ways enquiry – not certainty – powered human progress from Socrates to the age of AI. Today she reveals how asking ‘why?’ enhances every conversation and relationship in our lives. Join us – there’ll be plenty of time for questions. Chaired by Sarah Manavis.

events.title: Celebrating Zoë Wicomb: Writing Between Worlds
events.blurb: Beloved writer, teacher, and thinker Zoë Wicomb transformed South African and Scottish literature with work of extraordinary intelligence, nuance, and moral clarity. In this special tribute event, we honour the life and work of the author of You Can’t Get Lost in Cape Town, David’s Story, and Still Life, celebrating her voice, her influence, and the enduring power of work that reshaped how we understand home, history, and belonging. Join friends and colleagues including Louise Welsh and Chitra Ramaswamy to discuss this astonishing individual.

events.title: Mikhail Fishman & Martin Sixsmith: Fear and Loathing in the Kremlin
events.blurb: As new wars flare elsewhere, Russia’s attacks on Ukraine haven’t abated since 2022's full-scale invasion, and began well before it. Hear unique and urgent perspectives on how we got here from exiled Russian journalist Mikhail Fishman, whose The Successor charts Russia’s decline from 1990 to 2015 through the life of assassinated activist and opposition leader, Boris Nemtsov – and Russia expert and former BBC Moscow correspondent, Martin Sixsmith, whose Suing the Kremlin documents efforts to recover the oligarch era’s lost billions. Chaired by Caroline Eden

events.title: Close Read: The Driver's Seat by Muriel Spark
events.blurb: In our Close Read series, a brilliant author guides you through a deep-diving discussion of a classic text or genre that’s inspired them. Think of it as an event blending friendly book club vibes with insightful study notes. Today, James Bailey (author of Like a Cat Loves a Bird) unpacks Muriel Spark’s metaphysical ‘whydunnit’, The Driver's Seat. With Bailey’s expert insight into the author’s life, get closer to Spark’s globetrotting tale of self-destruction.

events.title: Angharad Hampshire & Katja Hoyer: What Would You Do?
events.blurb: The Mare – journalist Angharad Hampshire’s Walter Scott Prize-shortlisted debut novel – is a gripping portrait of an ordinary woman’s descent into inhumanity during World War II. Historian Katja Hoyer’s Weimar: Life on the Edge of Catastrophe draws on archival research to explore the true story of how, as the war enveloped them, the inhabitants of the ancient German town of Weimar became  witnesses, perpetrators, victims, and bystanders. Together they discuss what we’re all capable of when faced with catastrophe. Chaired by Alexander Starritt.

events.title: Tim Key: L.A. Baby!
events.blurb: Following packed-out events with us in 2024 and 2025, comedian and writer Tim Key returns to the Festival with poetry collection, L.A. Baby!, created with his long-time design collaborator, Emily Juniper. Described by the Guardian as ‘a hilarious and dreamlike chronical’, Key’s latest collection constantly finds and pokes fun at the gild of Hollywood. Join Key for an hour of laugh-out-loud poetry and anecdotes about his hectic adventures during his time cast adrift in La-La Land. Chaired by Rhys James.

events.title: Cecilia Knapp & Lisa Owens: Girl, Woman, Mother?
events.blurb: In Lack, Cecilia Knapp writes a woman grappling with uncertainty about bringing new life into a burning world. In Natural Disaster, Lisa Owens follows a woman across the final 24 hours of parental leave, capturing the literal and existential challenges of being a mother, employee, and partner. Hear the authors discussing how their novels, from opposite sides of motherhood, speak to each other and to the push and pull of what it means to be a woman today. Chaired by Cailean Steed.

events.title: Claudia Rankine: Triage
events.blurb: Genre-defying, multi-awarding-winning poet, essayist, and playwright Claudia Rankine returns to the Festival to discuss her remarkable new work, Triage. Through a hypnotic blend of narrative, memoir, and imagery, the novel follows a turbulent friendship that’s buckled under the weight of the world. In this special event, Rankine speaks with Marjorie Lotfi about how beautiful, complicated friendships help us make sense of our lives and that in the midst of anger, and exhaustion, there is hope.

events.title: Get Your Graphic Novel Started with Chanté Timothy
events.blurb: Chanté Timothy is a brilliant graphic novelist – the creator of the award-winning series about a brainy young super-scientist, Supa Nova. If you’ve always dreamed of getting your own stories down on the page, Chanté’s here to help you on your way with a gentle introduction to storytelling through illustration. Whether you're already an art whizz, or just want to do stick figure comics, Chanté knows how to get those sketches story ready.

events.title: A Kick Up the Arts with Nicola Meighan – Live
events.blurb: Arts writer and broadcaster supreme Nicola Meighan (BBC Radio Scotland, BBC Radio 4, The Herald) presents a live recording of her popular arts and culture podcast, A Kick Up the Arts, where she’s hosted guests ranging from Val McDermid and Deacon Blue to Irvine Welsh and Barbara Dickson, as well as countless other brilliant voices. Enjoy an hour of live music and deep dive into albums, films, and books with some truly special guests. With Kathryn Joseph and Lomond Campbell. Kirstin Innes is now participating in this event.

events.title: Gwendoline Riley: The Palm House
events.blurb: Nobody writes the humour and pathos of ordinary lives quite like Gwendoline Riley, recently awarded the prestigious Windham-Campbell Prize. In The Palm House, she turns her unerring ear and razor-sharp wit to a long friendship weathering bereavement, bad bosses, and old hurts that still bite. Talking with Sinéad Gleeson today, Riley (author of First Love and My Phantoms) brings her eviscerating powers of observation to discuss her portrait of enduring friendship and a meeting of minds.

events.title: Liam Byrne, Sarah Stein Lubrano & Marius Ostrowski: Can You Change Your Mind?
events.blurb: How did we get so entrenched in our political and ideological positions? Can we change other people’s minds about anything? And what does our newfound certainty about everything mean for society, for politics, and for our relationships? MP Liam Byrne (Why Populists Are Winning: and How to Beat Them), writer and researcher Sarah Stein Lubrano (Don’t Talk About Politics: How to Change 21st Century Minds), and historian Marius Ostrowski (How We Think: Ten Thinker-Types to Understand Ourselves and Those Around Us) explore these critical questions, and more. Chaired by Talat Yaqoob.

events.title: Nonomiya/Song of Rona Island
events.blurb:
As part of Scotland to the World, we bring you a unique fusion of Japanese and Scottish culture. Rarely experienced outside its home country, Noh is a 600-year-old form of classical Japanese musical drama, into which the experimental Noh Reimagined theatre company is breathing new life. They bring us today’s two-part performance, introducing Noh Theatre in Part One with Nonomiya - a piece based on the oldest novel of all time, followed by Song of Rona Island - a new and contemporary collaboration, based on Kathleen Jamie's essay 'On Rona', which blends Scottish and Japanese folklore, myth and music, in Part Two. Full line-up includes Kanji Shimizu, Takao Nishimura, Kyosuke Tanabe, Satoshi Tsukitaku, Keinosuke Okura, Aidan O’Rourke & Brighde Chaimbeul.
Note: This is a repeat of the performance on Mon 24 Aug at 19:00.

events.title: The Front List: Special Edition – John Grisham
events.blurb: The original legal thriller sensation, John Grisham has written 52 consecutive number one bestsellers, which have sold 500 million copies in more than 45 languages around the world. Chances are you’ll find a copy of The Client, The Rainmaker, or A Time To Kill on your own bookshelf – or you'll have caught one of his blockbuster film adaptations starring Tom Cruise (The Firm) or Julia Roberts (The Pelican Brief). As a prominent advocate for criminal justice reform, Grisham is an active supporter of organisations dedicated to exonerating those who have been wrongfully convicted. In today’s rare and special event, Grisham speaks to award-winning crime writer Ian Rankin about his incredible career, the state of the US criminal justice system, and the relationship between the high-stakes fiction and stark reality of the law.

events.title: Kim Sherwood: James Bond — Hurricane Room
events.blurb: What’s it like to write one of the world’s most famous characters? Commissioned by the Ian Fleming Estate to expand on the James Bond canon, Kim Sherwood’s trilogy comes to an explosive conclusion with Hurricane Room. Lauded for how her Double O novels ‘feel both as old as time and fresh and new’ (John Yorke), Sherwood returns to the Festival to talk about the beloved spy saga on the cusp of the final showdown. Chaired by Dan Richards.

events.title: Daniel Kehlmann: The Director
events.blurb: Hollywood to Nazi Germany, Garbo to Goebbels – The Director is Daniel Kehlmann’s imaginative take on filmmaker G W Pabst and the heady entanglement of art, politics, and power at the peak of the Nazi regime. Exploring complicity and moral compromise, the rise and fall of German cinema, and the politics and propaganda of the silver screen, don’t miss International Booker Prize-shortlisted Kehlmann discussing his controversial, magnificent book, and his storied career with our Festival director, Jenny Niven.

events.title: The Book That Changed My Mind
events.blurb: Books can soothe, expand, and stimulate our minds – but can they change them completely? In this thought-provoking panel event - chaired by journalist and Emeritus Director of the International Booker Prize, Fiammetta Rocco - incredible authors encourage us to reflect on the turning-point books that shape our worldviews. Compare notes with Kiran Desai (The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny) and Claudia Rankine (Triage) on the revelatory books in their literary lives.

events.title: GUBSMACKED: Flyte Nyte 2026
events.blurb: Like the modern rap battle, ‘flytings’ flourished in 15th century Scotland as a form of entertainment, and as a means of garnering respect, attention, and speaking truth to power. Today, GUBSMACKED return to the Festival with the dazzlingly rude and boisterous Flyte Nyte! Join your hosts, Colin Bramwell, Leyla Josephine, and Iona Lee, and witness poets, rappers, and spoken word artists such as Murid Laly, Sean Wai Keung, Taylor Dyson, Billy Letford, Elvis MacGonagoll and Medha Singhall, all fighting to become the evening’s Flyting Champion using nothing but wit, verse, extravagant verbal abuse, and name-calling – bring it on!

events.title: Are You Sitting Comfortably?
events.blurb: Join us for a relaxed morning story especially for your littlest readers. Check website for today's author.

events.title: First Edition
events.blurb: Start your day with the facts. High quality, thorough, trustworthy journalism has never been more important in helping us understand the world as it really is – but we know how hard it can be to keep up. That’s what our First Edition events are for: offering you the chance to join leading journalists, including Nicolas Niarchos, from across the media (and the world) as they discuss the day’s breaking news over a cup of coffee. Check back soon for the full line-up. Chaired by Paul French.

events.title: Shared Reading with Open Book
events.blurb: Join Open Book Lead Readers for an informal and relaxed shared reading session. Each session will explore a chapter from a debut book from this year’s Festival programme. No experience necessary, all reading materials will be provided on the day.

events.title: James Bailey: The Nine Lives of Muriel Spark
events.blurb: 20 years have passed since the death of Scottish literary icon Muriel Spark, and in 2027, Edinburgh will see a new statue installed in her honour. James Bailey, in Like a Cat Loves a Bird, captures the essence of Spark’s chaotic and remarkable life. As we sit just a stone's throw from the Miss Jean Brodie Steps, Bailey shares an enthralling insight on the woman behind Edinburgh’s most formidable schoolteacher. Chaired by Susan Mansfield.

events.title: The Front List: Mel Giedroyc
events.blurb: Comedian, presenter, and Sunday Times bestselling author Mel Giedroyc is at the peak of her powers… unlike Gill, the central character of The Comeback. A failed performer who spies a chance at creative glory by staging a spectacular show to celebrate her local theatre’s 100th anniversary, Gill finds herself at war with a diva Artistic Director who wants to draw the curtain early. In what’s set to be a Festival highlight, join Giedroyc for a big-hearted chat about dreams, drama, and community with none other than comedian, author, and Giedroyc’s lifelong pal and comedy partner, Sue Perkins.

events.title: Close Read with Open Book: The News from Dublin by Colm Tóibín
events.blurb: Join Jess Orr and Claire Urquhart from Open Book, a charity organising shared reading and creative groups, as they lead a warm, lively discussion on Colm Tóibín’s breathtaking new short story collection, The News from Dublin. Dig into these subtle, powerful stories of longing, loss, and life far from home by the renowned author of Brooklyn. No preparation required, reading materials will be provided. Expect an open discussion from the start.

events.title: Juno Dawson & Daisy Dixon: When Art Offends
events.blurb: Prize-winning philosopher Daisy Dixon’s Depraved: The Story of Dangerous Art takes readers through some of history’s most contentious artworks. Meanwhile, bestselling author Juno Dawson knows firsthand what it’s like to be the target of censorship; her 2014 YA title, This Book is Gay, is listed as one of the most frequently banned books in the USA. Today, the pair discuss the ‘morality’ of art, and why what we choose to condemn reveals so much about us. Chaired by Sarah Manavis.

events.title: Jennifer Higgie: Bedlam
events.blurb: A painter of fairies, a deranged murderer, and an inmate of history’s most notorious insane asylum: Victorian artist Richard Dadd is the mesmerising subject of Jennifer Higgie’s ‘dream-fever’ of a novel, Bedlam. Former editor of Frieze magazine, Turner Prize judge, and celebrated author of The Other Side, Higgie brings her formidable art critic’s intelligence to an enthralling conversation with Di Speirs about art and illness, vision and delusion, and the transcendent, unsettling power of paint.

events.title: Beyond Borders: Women in Conflict
events.blurb: The Women in Conflict 1325 Fellowship - run by Beyond Borders Scotland in partnership with the University of Edinburgh Law School and funded by the Scottish Government – brings together women from all over the world who are working at the frontlines of peacemaking and conflict resolution. Hear some of their remarkable stories, connecting the dots between conflict resolution, climate, and human rights, and explore Scotland’s ambitions to bring together organisations involved in peace and reconciliation. Khulood al Saidi, Alaa Assani and Shatha Altowai are the panelists for this event. Chaired by Roxani Krystalli.

events.title: Non-Fiction Reporting: A Workshop with Sally Hayden
events.blurb: Orwell Prize-winning journalist Sally Hayden (This is Also a Love Story) leads you through how to turn non-fiction reporting into a book, in a workshop that’ll get you thinking about how to nail the start, end, and overall structure. This is a rare opportunity to ask one of our finest journalists – who’s covered migration, conflict, and humanitarian crises throughout her career – your burning questions on everything from book proposals to the editing process. Ideal for those who’ve already done some research into their topic of interest.

events.title: Peter Meades & Frank Tallis: Midlife, Masculinity, and Meaning
events.blurb: How do you keep going when the old ways of coping no longer work? Clinical psychologist Frank Tallis and integrative psychotherapist Peter Meades approach this question from complementary angles: Tallis through the psychology of aging, Meades through the current crisis in men’s mental health. With Wise and I’m Fine (But Not Really), the authors bring compassion and insight to a conversation with Jamie Jauncey about aging well, expectations around ‘masculinity’, and finding new paths towards resilience.

events.title: Tahmima Anam & Balsam Karam: Stand Up, Fight Back
events.blurb: Two masters of their craft, Tahmima Anam and Balsam Karam, weave stories of resistance and solidarity in their latest novels. In Anam’s Uprising, Kusum is brought to an island of subjugated women, sparking rebellion when she refuses to yield to power. In Karam’s Event Horizon, Milde must choose between execution or an experimental space mission to an uncharted black hole. Join these bold writers discussing how fiction can help us imagine alternative ways to live. Chaired by Rachelle Atalla.

events.title: The Ukraine Shelf: What to Read about Ukraine
events.blurb: In the fifth year of Russia’s full-scale invasion, The Ukraine Shelf podcast brings together leading writers and thinkers for lively, informed discussion on what we should be reading to better understand Ukraine during this crucial period. Today, the hosts – Olesya Khromeychuk (director of the Ukrainian Institute London and author of The Death of a Soldier Told by His Sister) and literary translator and scholar Uilleam Blacker – chat to Ukraine’s Deputy Minister of Culture and journalist Bohdana Laiuk, and Guardian chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins, author of Ukrainian Lessons: Art in a Time of War.

events.title: Gabriella Bennett & Bruce Peter: Designs for Life
events.blurb: From bomb-resistant bedrooms in Ukraine to hidden Art Deco gems in Glasgow, architecture reveals so much about the society it serves. Gabriella Bennett, journalist and author of How to Build a City, sits down with Bruce Peter, Professor of Design History at Glasgow School of Art and author of Art Deco Scotland, for an illuminating discussion about buildings as portals to the past – and blueprints for a better future. Chaired by Leonie Bell.

events.title: Tracy Borman: The House of Boleyn
events.blurb: In her novel The House of Boleyn, Tracy Borman, Chief Historian at Historic Royal Palaces, brings the Boleyns’ calculated rise and swift fall to vivid life in their most intimate and unwitnessed space: Hever Castle. Exploring the relationships and conversations not captured in conventional history books, Borman joins Vic Murray to discuss the secrets, danger, and passion which drove a family and changed the country forever, all absorbed by the walls of their home.

events.title: The Kitchen Book: A Table Talk with Ella Risbridger
events.blurb:
Ella Risbridger is as deft with a pen as she is with a spatula, a writer who can turn a recipe for Marmite soup into stomach-rumbling poetry. Watch her rustle up something hearty from The Kitchen Book, her cooking companion that promises to make every meal ‘10% better’, then listen to her wax lyrical about food as the purest form of happiness. Ticket includes: a welcome drink and a delicious food taster. Chaired by Nyla Ahmad.

Age limit: 18+

events.title: Angela Flournoy & Claudia Rankine: How Do You Write About America?
events.blurb: Two exquisite writers, Angela Flournoy (The Turner House, The Wilderness) and Claudia Rankine (the American trilogy, Triage), parse the problems and potential of writing about contemporary America. Both unflinching in their interrogation of its culture, politics, and deep inequalities, today they come together for a frank conversation about why their homeland stays at the centre of their work, and what the freedom of fiction, poetry, and narrative essay reveals about America that other forms cannot. Chaired by Dina Nayeri.

events.title: Sue Black: An Expert Witness
events.blurb: World-leading anatomist and forensic anthropologist Sue Black is no stranger to putting her reputation on the line in the name of justice. Now, in An Expert Witness, she puts forensic science on trial to understand where it sits in the judicial balance, and just how little it can take to make or break a verdict. Hear Black talking with us about how, in seismic events, the answers often lie in the smallest of details. Chaired by Peggy Hughes.

events.title: Finding Your People with L D Lapinski
events.blurb: When labels just don’t fit, life’s rarely smooth sailing. Or smooth skating, as is the case in L D Lapinski’s Kickflip. The thoughtful graphic novel follows non-binary teen Elliot as they struggle to merge school life with their passion for skateboarding. Join Lapinski for a unique event about friendship, writing, and the sheer joy of being able to express yourself creatively. There’ll also be time to meet and chat with like-minded folk afterwards!

events.title: Nicolas Niarchos & Alex Perry: Blood & Oil
events.blurb: We’re all aware of the environmental cost of using fossil fuels to power our lives, but the human and cultural impact is arguably just as damaging. In Blood Will Flow, investigative journalist Alex Perry illuminates the dark underbelly of the oil industry through a massacre in Mozambique, while The New Yorker writer Nicolas Niarchos’ The Elements of Power examines the bloody history of cobalt, from Congolese mines to our phone batteries. Chaired by Sally Hayden.

events.title: Russell Tovey: Starlings
events.blurb: A leading light on our screens for decades, Russell Tovey is known for roles in everything from The History Boys to American Horror Story. Now, the beloved actor and co-host of the popular Talk Art podcast is set to debut his Audible Original novel, featuring a cast led by Andrew Scott and George MacKay. He joins us to chat about Starlings, a beautiful coming-of-age story of identity and estrangement centring on the reconciliation of two brothers. Chaired by Barry Pierce.

events.title: Let's Write! with the Scottish Book Trust
events.blurb: Our pals at Scottish Book Trust – inventor of the New Writers Awards – know all about writing, and what you need to take that next step to publication. In this interactive session, they’ll be offering top tips, exercises, and excellent chat which could help on your writing journey. Presented by Scottish Book Trust.

events.title: Bryony Gordon: People Pleaser
events.blurb: Sunday Times bestseller Bryony Gordon adds ‘debut novelist’ to her impressive skillset with People Pleaser. The hugely popular author of The Wrong Knickers, host of The Life of Bryony podcast, Daily Mail columnist, and award-winning mental health campaigner, Gordon now takes a laugh-'til-you-cry look at pleasing everyone else… then saying NO. Hear one of our most honest stars discuss why women don't often do this – and the joy of breaking free. Chaired by Claire Sawers.

events.title: Scott Anderson: King of Kings
events.blurb: In 1978, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, the Shah of Iran, entertained US President Jimmy Carter in Tehran where they congratulated themselves on a peaceful period in both their countries. A year later, the Shah was dethroned in a violent revolution led by the exiled Ayatollah Khomeini and his supporters. Pulitzer Prize shortlistee Scott Anderson joins us to discuss King of Kings, a finely-researched, thrilling account of the last days of the Shah’s regime and how it set the tone for US-Iran relations to this day. Chaired by Dina Nayeri.

events.title: Long Day? Cook This: A Table Talk with Justin Tsang
events.blurb:
Justin Tsang’s Long Day? Cook This is the sort of book that’ll stay permanently open in your kitchen, bursting with easy East Asian recipes that taste anything but: firecracker rice, tangy instant noodle salad, and kimchi egg ribbon udon soup. Watch ‘Justin the Dustbin’ (his moniker on socials) whip up a treat as he chats flavour pairings, kitchen shortcuts, and cutting his teeth at his family’s Chinese restaurant. Ticket includes: a welcome drink and a delicious food taster. Chaired by Sean Wai Keung.

Age limit: 18+

events.title: Spartans: The Way We See It
events.blurb: Join us to celebrate a collection of amazing work from young people reflecting their experiences of the world and their place in it. Original, imaginative writing and personal manifestos combine to give us a look at life through the eyes of the bright, brave, and brilliant pupils who attend Spartans Community Foundation’s Alternative School.  This event is a collaboration between the young people and the Book Festival’s Writers in Residence, Owen Sutcliffe and Chris Barkley.

events.title: Anand Gopal: Days of Love and Rage
events.blurb: In 2011, in the Syrian city of Manbij, a small group of individuals began a movement that overthrew a brutal dictatorship. Pulitzer Prize-finalist and The New Yorker journalist Anand Gopal’s Days of Love and Rage is a sweeping account of Syrians fighting for a better world and in doing so, undertaking one of the most remarkable experiments in democracy of modern times. Less than two years after the Assad regime’s fall, Gopal discusses his masterful work that’s gained comparisons to Phillip Gouretvich and Katherine Boo. Chaired by Henry Bell.

events.title: Andrey Kurkov: Telling the Truth
events.blurb: One of Ukraine’s finest novelists (and he’s written 19 of them!), Andrey Kurkov also writes vividly about the personal, political, and social cost of the invasion of his home country. Today, we’re honoured to welcome him back to talk both fact and fiction: discussing the third instalment of his International Booker Prize-longlisted Kyiv Mysteries series, The Lost Soldiers, alongside the third volume of his war diaries, Three Years on Fire, chronicling the third year of Russia’s invasion. Chaired by Rosie Goldsmith.

events.title: Hamish Hawk: Life in a Scotch Sitting Room, Vol. 0 – The Encore
events.blurb: After two sold out 2025 performances and a packed UK tour, local indie hero Hamish Hawk returns to the Spiegeltent with with his mesmerising Book Festival-commissioned Life in a Scotch Sitting Room, Vol. 0 for a very special homecoming performance. Blending his own take on some of Scottish poet eccentric Ivor Cutler’s iconic works with his own original passages and compositions, don’t miss your last chance to enjoy what’s bound to be one of the hottest tickets in this year’s programme.

events.title: Are You Sitting Comfortably?
events.blurb: Join us for a relaxed morning story especially for your littlest readers. Check website for today's author.

events.title: First Editions: International Reporting
events.blurb: Start your day with the facts. High quality, thorough, trustworthy journalism has never been more important in helping us understand the world as it really is – but we know how hard it can be to keep up. That’s what our First Edition events are for: offering you the chance to join leading journalists from across the media (and the world) as they discuss the day’s breaking news over a cup of coffee. Today’s guests include the BBC’s chief international correspondent, Lyse Doucet, journalist and foreign correspondent Sally Hayden, and Jen Stout. Chaired by Halla Mohieddeen.

events.title: Ways of Seeing Food: A Writing Workshop with Tamar Adler
events.blurb: Tamar Adler – author of An Everlasting Meal and Feast on Your Life – is adored among chefs and home cooks alike for her rhapsodic writing about food. Today, she invites you for a special masterclass on how to approach food writing sideways. Through writing exercises and open discussion, Adler guides you through how to render food beyond its taste and texture, exploring the symbolism, memories, and emotional weight it carries. With fresh coffee and baked goods on hand, just bring your creativity.

events.title: Jacek Dukaj & Ursula Phillips: Ice
events.blurb: In Jacek Dukaj's Ice, the Tunguska asteroid has plunged the world into eternal winter, freezing not just the land but history itself. A Polish mathematician is sent deep into a transformed Siberia - and into one of the most inventive alternate histories ever written. Joining Dukaj is translator Ursula Phillips, whose remarkable English translation navigates the novel’s intricate tensions between Polish, Russian, and a deranged reality. Together they explore the art of carrying audacious imagined worlds across languages. Chaired by Uilleam Blacker.

events.title: The Front List: Lyse Doucet
events.blurb: As the BBC’s Chief International Correspondent, Lyse Doucet has witnessed 30 years of seismic events at dangerously close quarters. With The Finest Hotel in Kabul: A People’s History of Afghanistan, she’s also been shortlisted for 2026’s Women’s Prize for Nonfiction. Examining decades of deadly political tumult in Afghanistan through the story of the Hotel Intercontinental and its extraordinary staff, join journalist Sally Hayden for a critical conversation with Doucet about current global events – drawing on her experience in global postings from Tehran to Abidjan – and their potential future outcomes.

events.title: Graphic Novels with Lizzy Stewart
events.blurb: Lizzy Stewart (author-illustrator of the breathtaking, genre-defying books The Wreck, Alison, and Walking Distance) introduces you today to the world of graphic storytelling. During this session, you’ll look at character, how to find inspiration, and the way that time can bend and stretch within a graphic novel or comic book. All of this will come together in a short-form comic strip which could form the basis of your own future full-length masterpiece.

events.title: Alex Hyde & Lisa Tuttle: Artist Turned Object
events.blurb: When art and obsession coalesce, the blurred lines can quickly become sinister. Alex Hyde’s Exhibition follows a photographer drawn into the intoxicating world of her artist best friend, with destructive results. Lisa Tuttle’s My Death is a rollercoaster of a novella about a writer’s exploration of an artist forgotten by history. Join them for a discussion on their uncanny works, asking questions about the sometimes dark, always complex relationship between art, identity, and authenticity. Chaired by Octavia Bright.

events.title: Louis de Bernières: Smelling of Rooks
events.blurb: Known for his tender and spirited writing, Louis de Bernières has built a reputation as one of the UK’s finest novelists. With his memoir, Smelling of Rooks, the author of Captain Corelli’s Mandolin turns the lens on himself, offering a portrait of a writer’s life in rural Norfolk. Today, he joins us for a conversation about gathering a decade of reflections on everything from cats to politics, and the unpredictable joys of country living. Chaired by Rosie Goldsmith.

events.title: Train Tales
events.blurb: Let's take a train to Imagination Land! Join our pals from LNER for Train Tales, a chance to hop aboard for stories and brilliant activities to help little ones get ready for future journeys. There might even be a very special guest...

events.title: Prue Leith: Being Old and Learning to Love It
events.blurb: Only the lucky grow old – so why is the thought of aging filled with fear and judgement for so many? Former judge of The Great British Bake Off and culinary legend Prue Leith, author of Being Old and Learning to Love It, is on a mission to change that. As a modern woman in her eighties, nothing is off-limits, as she shares the many unexpected joys of getting older, as well as its taboos. Join Leith for a discussion full of wit, wisdom, and her trademark no-nonsense charm. Chaired by Sam Baker.

events.title: Lucy Ash: Russia’s Church from Pagans to Putin
events.blurb: Moving away from the atheism of the 20th century’s Soviet Union, Putin’s Russia has granted the ancient Russian Orthodox Church great power. BBC reporter and Russia expert Lucy Ash joins us to discuss her provocative new book, The Baton and the Cross, a finalist for both the Orwell and British Academy Book Prizes. Hear her unpack Russian Orthodoxy’s history and how, under Putin, religion is being stripped of its spirituality, used instead as a weapon of control. Chaired by Misha Glenny.

events.title: Caden Armstrong, Nadine Aisha Jassat & Ella Risbridger: Love on the Brain
events.blurb: Slow burns and bodice rippers, unrequited yearning and enemies-to-lovers: romantic fiction contains whole universes of passion, pain, and stomach-flipping chemistry. Its domination of bestseller lists proves we all want a little more love in our lives, so join this celebration of our culture’s most enduring genre, featuring In Love with Love author Ella Risbridger, Edinburgh’s Book Lovers Bookshop owner Caden Armstrong, and poet, author, and avid romance-reader Nadine Aisha Jassat. Chaired by Alisha Fernandez Miranda.

events.title: Hannah Lavery, Jennifer Wong & Nidhi Zak/Aria Eipe: Migratory Patterns
events.blurb: Jennifer Wong’s Light Year is a moving, generation-spanning examination of family history. Hannah Lavery’s Everything Everyday is both witness and archive, putting shape on a year of chaos and upheaval. Nidhi Zak/Aria Eipe’s Auguries of a Minor God is a skilful, profound account of home, migration, and exile. These extraordinary poets come together in conversation to discuss their practice and how they articulate the matter of human migration into poetry, song, and myth. Chaired by Catherine Wilson Garry.

events.title: Louise Newson: The Power of Hormones
events.blurb: When it comes to women’s health, there’s a long and harmful history of misdiagnosis, medical blindness, and complacency. In today’s myth-busting conversation, hormone specialist Dr Louise Newson – a leading authority on menopause care, as well as a Sunday Times bestselling author, host of the UK’s no.1 medical podcast (The Dr Louise Newson Podcast), and founder of the Balance app – unpacks her bold new book, The Power of Hormones. Kylie Reid – founder and director of Scottish women’s network, egg – chairs this insightful, urgent discussion about how better understanding our hormones could radically transform our lives.

events.title: Feast on Your Life: A Table Talk with Tamar Adler
events.blurb: Feast on Your Life sums up Tamar Adler’s philosophy: that cooking can be a devotion, a way to bring life-affirming joy to even the most mundane days. Today she whips us up something delicious as she shares her meditations on food as self-love, the power of a passed-down recipe, and the most meaningful meals of her life. You’ll leave seeing your kitchen in a warm new light. Chaired by Marjorie Lotfi. Ticket includes: a welcome drink and a delicious food taster.

events.title: Ana Kinsella & Lizzy Stewart: Feelings and Faultlines
events.blurb: In Frida Slattery as Herself – Ana Kinsella’s absorbing love letter to artistic expression – an actor and director walk a messy line between collaboration and connection. In The Wreck, the literary graphic novel from illustrator Lizzy Stewart, undercurrents and double standards are laid bare when two creative couples experiment in communal living. Together, they’ll dive into the long-simmering tensions that underpin many of our so-called closest relationships and what’s really acceptable in the name of art. Chaired by Barry Pierce.

events.title: Mariana Mazzucato: The Common Good Economy
events.blurb: What if our economy served the whole planet, and not just the few? An acclaimed Professor of Economics and policy advisor, honoured by both the Pope and King for her work, Mariana Mazzucato’s The Common Good Economy draws on decades of expertise to offer a systemic reinvention – creating a space for us all to flourish.
